# Discussion

Although PISA and ICILS differ in their strategies for measuring DSE, a reduced scales in both studies reviewed demonstrate clear two-dimensional behavior. The items that were eliminated reveals important trends to consider for innovating future measurements.Some tasks that do not belong to the basic set of digital literacy (i.e. information, communication, and creation) did not fit into the proposed two-dimensional model, anchored to a linear distinction of the degree of difficulty of the tasks to group the factors. For example, expectations for achieving changes in device settings, specific to managing user ‘privacy,’ distort the model in both studies. Likewise, other tasks did not seem to have the same meaning that students had given them in previous measurements. While in previous versions of these studies, web page development was a clearly distinctive skill of specialized technology users, the results suggest that it shares considerable variance with the latent construct of general self-efficacy. The opposite is true for multimedia content creation, which has moved from general self-efficacy to a blurred area between the two dimensions. Technological contexts change over time. It is likely that new developments in digital tools have brought some tasks that were previously challenging for the general public closer together, while other tasks that previously appeared to be simple have become more complex than usual.

The factor analysis confirms that it is possible to obtain a common scale from the data that is relatively comparable across cultures and by gender. ICILS present moderate problems with scalar invariance adjustments by country, which can be explained because the different understandings of self-efficacy behind the strategies of measuring. Since PISA tends to give a context of difficulty to the construct, which involves the development of logical thinking and a social context behind it, it achieves better levels of adjustment than ICILS, a study that focuses on the performance achievement of tasks in abstract. By introducing less information, cultural differences are likely to differentiate the way students from different countries interpret the meaning of the question.

In both studies, overall countries demonstrate major levels of general than specialized self-efficacy. The gender mean distribution of general self-efficacy show minimal gaps in favor of girls, while specialized self-efficacy favors boys to a considerable extent. A Counterintutive result points that less developed countries as Kazakhstan or Romania present the best specialized scores, in spite of their bad peformance on general self-efficacy. At the same time, catches the attention the reduced or neutralized gender specialized self-efficacy gap of global-south countries as Chile, Korea, Kazakhstan, where policies aimed at encouraging STEM engagement on girls are supposedly less intense than the global-north countries, where the gap tend to be higher. The consistency between the two studies confirms a recent trend within gender and STEM literature: the paradox that in countries with less gender equality, attitudinal differences between men and women tend to decrease [@marsh_illusory_2021;@guo_crosscultural_2024].

# Conclussions

The present article demonstrate that, even though PISA and ICILS propose different dimensional approach to digital self-efficacy, a comparative bi-dimensional scale (based on the linear difficulty of the task) between the two studies can be proposed.
